concepts.title: Scenarios for Homography: Planar Scenes and Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: A homography is a simple geometric transformation that maps pixels between images when the scene is planar or the camera undergoes pure rotation.
concepts.content:
In general, mapping pixels between two images from different viewpoints requires knowing the 3D scene structure and relative camera motion. However, in specific scenarios, a simple transformation called a homography can warp one image into another without 3D knowledge. This occurs when the scene is planar or when the two cameras are related only by a rotation. 

[FIGURE:d89ebe83f072de38]

[FIGURE:4c2d17b07db71aed]

These two images are (approximately) related by an homography. Homographies are used in applications such as perspective correction, augmented reality, image stitching, and creating bird's-eye views.
concepts.motivation_md: Homographies simplify image alignment by removing the need for complex 3D reconstruction in common cases like stitching panoramas or correcting the perspective of a flat document.
concepts.recap_md:
- Homographies apply when the scene is planar or the camera motion is pure rotation.
 - They allow image warping without requiring explicit 3D scene structure.
 - Common applications include image stitching and perspective correction.

key_passage.text: there are a few scenarios where we can find a simple transformation that allows warping one image into another image corresponding to a new camera location without requiring knowing the 3D scene structure: this will happen when the scene is planar or when the two cameras are related just by a rotation. In those two cases the coordinates of corresponding points across the two images are related by a homography.

motivation.text: Homographies can be used in applications such as perspective correction, augmented reality, image stitching, creating bird's-eye views, correcting keystone distortions for projected images, and many others.

concepts.title: Definition of Homography (Projective Transformation)
concepts.one_liner: A homography, or projective transformation, is a geometric transformation that preserves the collinearity of points and can be represented by a 3x3 matrix multiplication in homogeneous coordinates.
concepts.content:
A homography (or projective transformation) is a geometric transformation that preserves straight lines. It is a function $h$ that maps points such that if points $\mathbf{p}_1$, $\mathbf{p}_2$, and $\mathbf{p}_3$ are collinear, their transformed versions $h(\mathbf{p}_1)$, $h(\mathbf{p}_2)$, and $h(\mathbf{p}_3)$ are also collinear. In homogeneous coordinates, this mapping $\mathbf{p}' = h(\mathbf{p})$ is expressed as a product with a $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{H}$:

$$\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ w' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & i \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

This is written compactly as $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}$, where $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{p}'$ are 2D points in homogeneous coordinates.

(see figure: Homography. Colinear points remain colinear after transformation. Angles between lines are not preserved.)
concepts.motivation_md: Defining homographies mathematically using matrices allows us to use linear algebra to efficiently transform images and solve for camera parameters.
concepts.recap_md:
- A homography preserves straight lines (collinearity) but not necessarily angles.
 - It is represented by a $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{H}$ acting on homogeneous coordinates.
 - The transformation is defined by the linear relation $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}$.

concepts.title: Proof of Collinearity Preservation under Homography
concepts.one_liner: Collinearity is preserved under homography because the linear equation of a line in homogeneous coordinates remains a linear equation after the transformation.
concepts.content: To prove that collinear points remain collinear after a homography, we use the equation of a line in homogeneous coordinates, $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}=0$. Given the homography relation $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{H} \mathbf{p}$, we can express the original points as $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{p}'$. Substituting this into the line equation yields $(\mathbf{H} ^{-\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{l})^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p'}=0$. This result is itself the equation of a line for the projected points $\mathbf{p}'$, confirming that they remain collinear.
concepts.motivation_md: This proof validates the fundamental property of homographies, ensuring that straight edges in the real world (like building corners) remain straight in warped images.
concepts.recap_md:
- The proof uses the homogeneous line equation $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}=0$.
 - Substituting $\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{p}'$ shows the transformed points satisfy a new line equation.
 - This confirms that projective transformations are indeed linear mappings in homogeneous space.

key_passage.text: To prove that colinear points remain colinear after the homography we can use the equation of a line in homogeneous coordinates, $\boldsymbol{l}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p}=0$. Replacing the last equality into the equation of the line gives $(\mathbf{H} ^{-\mathsf{T}}\boldsymbol{l})^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{p'}=0$, which corresponds to the equation of the line for the projected points $\mathbf{p}'$.

concepts.title: Homography from Camera Rotation
concepts.one_liner: The coordinates of corresponding points across images taken from the same point by rotating the camera are related by a homography, independently of their distance.
concepts.content:
When three images are taken from the same point by rotating the camera with no translation between positions, the coordinates of corresponding points are related by a homography. This relationship holds independently of how far the points are from the camera. 

[FIGURE:1db46673e5bbe185]

[FIGURE:8267e250a2c64ddf]

[FIGURE:83ad2f9f3b5c333e]

Setting the world coordinate system to align with camera 1, the projection of a 3D point $\mathbf{P}=[X,Y,Z]^\mathsf{T}$ into the camera 1 plane (with zero translation) is:
$$\lambda_1 \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{I} & \mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix}$$

Projecting the same point into camera 2 with rotation $\mathbf{R}$ and zero translation gives:
$$\lambda_2 \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{bmatrix}$$

(see figure: Camera rotation generates two images related by a homography.)

By inverting these projections, we find the relationship between corresponding image points in homogeneous coordinates:
$$\lambda_2 / \lambda_1 \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

This can be written as $\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{H} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$, where $\mathbf{H}$ is a $3\times3$ matrix. This relationship also holds if the two cameras have different intrinsic parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how images can be perfectly aligned or stitched together when the camera only rotates. It proves that for a purely rotating camera, the transformation between views is a simple linear mapping in homogeneous coordinates, which is essential for creating panoramas from a single tripod location.
concepts.recap_md: - Pure camera rotation (zero translation) results in image coordinates related by a $3\times3$ homography matrix.

key_passage.text: the coordinates of the corresponding points across each pair of images are related by a homography independently of how far they are from the camera.

motivation.text: The three images are taken from the same point by rotating the camera. There is no translation between the three camera positions as the photographer took the three images by keeping the camera origin static when moving the camera. Under this condition, the coordinates of the corresponding points across each pair of images are related by a homography independently of how far they are from the camera.

concepts.title: Homography from Planar Surfaces
concepts.one_liner: When two cameras observe a 2D plane, the coordinates of corresponding points inside that plane are related by a homography.
concepts.content:
When two cameras observe a 2D plane, the coordinates of corresponding points across the two views for points inside that plane are related by a homography. 

[FIGURE:8d12e88a6496cd81]

[FIGURE:d33152acf9add1c2]

To prove this, we place the world-coordinate system on the plane such that $Z=0$. 

(see figure: Geometry of a the projection of a planar scene. The origin of the world-coordinates system is placed inside the plane and the $Z$-axis is perpendicular to it.)

The projection equation for a camera is:
$$\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

By setting $Z=0$ for points on the plane, the equation simplifies to:
$$\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R} & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{c}_1 & \mathbf{c}_2 &\mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

where $\mathbf{c}_i$ is the $i$-th column of the rotation matrix $\mathbf{R}$. Since this is a product of two $3 \times 3$ matrices, it can be written as $\lambda \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{H} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Because this holds for any camera, the relationship between corresponding points in two cameras viewing the same plane is also a homography.
concepts.motivation_md: In many real-world scenes, such as buildings or roads, the geometry is dominated by flat surfaces. Understanding that planar surfaces map between views via a homography allows for tasks like perspective correction, document scanning, and augmented reality overlays on flat surfaces.
concepts.recap_md: - Points on a 3D plane map to image coordinates via a homography.

key_passage.text: This last result shows that the coordinates of points on the plane are related to the corresponding points in the image plane by a homography.

concepts.title: Homography vs Epipolar Constraint
concepts.one_liner: A homography is a stronger constraint than the epipolar constraint but only applies under specific conditions.
concepts.content: A homography is a stronger constraint than the epipolar constraint between corresponding points across two camera views. However, the homography only applies under certain conditions—such as a purely rotating camera or a planar scene—while the epipolar constraint always holds for any general motion and scene geometry.
concepts.motivation_md: It is important to distinguish between general geometric constraints (epipolar) and specific geometric constraints (homography). Knowing when to use a homography allows for more precise modeling when the scene is planar or the camera motion is restricted.
concepts.recap_md: - Homography is a stronger constraint than the epipolar constraint.

key_passage.text: A homography is a stronger constraint than the epipolar constraint between corresponding points across two camera views. However, the homography only applies under certain conditions as we have seen, while the epipolar constraint always holds.

concepts.title: Direct Linear Transform (DLT) for Homography Estimation
concepts.one_liner: The Direct Linear Transform (DLT) estimates a homography matrix from a set of point correspondences by solving a linear system.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Two overlapping images and some found correspondences using SURF descriptors. A random set of four correspondences are highlighted.)

Given a set of point correspondences across two cameras, we can compute the homography relating the locations of imaged points using the direct linear transform (DLT) algorithm. This results in a linear set of equations for the parameters of the homography matrix in the form $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{0}$, where $\mathbf{A}$ is a $2N \times 9$ matrix for $N$ corresponding pairs. 

The vector $\mathbf{h}$ contains the 9 elements of the matrix $\mathbf{H}$ stacked as a column vector. Since $\mathbf{h}$ has only 8 degrees of freedom (due to global scaling), at least four correspondences are required for estimation. The solution is the eigenvector of $\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}$ corresponding to the smallest eigenvalue, which minimizes the residual $\|\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} \|^2$. In practice, it is useful to further minimize the reprojection error after initialization with DLT, as the algebraic residual $\|\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} \|^2$ lacks geometric meaning.
concepts.motivation_md: To align images or map points between views, we need a mathematical method to calculate the transformation matrix. DLT provides a direct, linear way to solve for this matrix using simple point matches.
concepts.recap_md: - DLT solves $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{0}$ to estimate the $3 \times 3$ homography matrix.

concepts.title: RANSAC (Random Sampling with Consensus)
concepts.one_liner: RANSAC is a robust model-fitting algorithm that uses random sampling and consensus to handle data containing outliers.
concepts.content:
RANSAC, which stands for random sampling with consensus, is an algorithm used to fit models to data robustly, particularly when feature point detection is noisy or contains mismatches. 

The procedure is as follows:
1. Randomly select a sufficient set of datapoints to fit the parameters of a model (such as a line or a homography).
2. Compute the model parameters from this randomly sampled set.
3. Identify the inliers in the dataset—datapoints that fit the model within a specified tolerance.
4. Repeat this procedure $N$ times.
5. Compute a final model using the set of inliers corresponding to the largest consensus set found across all iterations.
concepts.motivation_md: In real-world computer vision, many point matches are incorrect (outliers). Standard least-squares methods fail in the presence of even a few outliers; RANSAC allows us to find the correct model by ignoring the 'noise'.
concepts.recap_md: - RANSAC fits models by repeatedly sampling small subsets of data and checking for consensus.

key_passage.text: First, randomly select a sufficient set of datapoints to fit the parameters of some model. Then, compute the model parameters from the randomly sampled set of points. Compute the inliers in the dataset, that is, the datapoints that fit the model (or achieve consensus) to within some tolerance. Repeat that procedure some number of times, N. Compute a final model from the set of inlier points corresponding to the largest number of inlier datapoints.

motivation.text: Because the detection of the feature points can be noisy, the homography fitting needs to be robust against inevitable feature mismatches between images. A good algorithm to fit models to data robustly is RANSAC, which stands for random sampling with concensus.

concepts.title: Heuristic for RANSAC Sample Count
concepts.one_liner: The number of RANSAC iterations required to find a good fit depends on the probability of selecting inliers and the desired confidence level.
concepts.content:
A heuristic can be derived for the number of samples $k$ required to ensure a good model fit with probability $p$. Let $n$ be the number of datapoints required to specify the model, and $w$ be the estimated probability that any selected datapoint is an inlier. 

The probability that all selected points in one trial are inliers is $w^n$, and the probability that at least one is an outlier is $1 - w^n$. The probability that only bad models are selected in $k$ trials is $(1 - w^n)^k$. Setting this equal to $1-p$ and solving for $k$ gives:
$$k = \frac{\log(1-p)}{\log(1-w^n)}$$

For example, if $w=0.18$ and $n=2$, achieving 95% accuracy requires $k=91$ trials. In practice, points should be selected without replacement to avoid degenerate fits, though the analysis assumes selection with replacement. This assumption is valid when the number of selected points is small relative to the total dataset.
concepts.motivation_md: Running RANSAC indefinitely is inefficient. This heuristic provides a mathematical way to determine the minimum number of iterations needed to be confident that we have found the correct model.
concepts.recap_md: - The number of iterations $k$ is calculated based on the inlier ratio $w$ and model size $n$.

concepts.title: Homography Estimation using RANSAC
concepts.one_liner: Homography estimation using RANSAC involves repeatedly sampling four point correspondences to robustly calculate the transformation matrix via DLT.
concepts.content: In the case of homography estimation, eight equations are required to use the DLT algorithm to estimate $\mathbf{H}$. Since each point correspondence contributes two equations, a minimum of four corresponding points is needed. To perform robust estimation, multiple sets of four points are randomly selected, and RANSAC is used to determine the homography that best fits the majority of the correspondences between two images.
concepts.motivation_md: Because feature matching often produces 'false positives' (points that look similar but aren't the same physical point), combining DLT with RANSAC is the standard way to reliably estimate a homography in real-world images.
concepts.recap_md: - Estimating a homography requires a minimum of four point correspondences.

key_passage.text: We can sample multiple randomly selected sets of four points and use RANSAC to estimate the homography between two images.

concepts.title: Image Stitching
concepts.one_liner: Image stitching uses estimated homographies to align and warp multiple overlapping images into a single panoramic view.
concepts.content:
Using DLT and RANSAC, the homography between each pair of images can be computed to align them with respect to a reference image. These estimated homographies allow for warping all images into a single camera view to create a panoramic image.

(see figure: Panoramic image composed by the three overlapping images from @fig-example_three_images)
concepts.motivation_md: Image stitching is the technology behind panoramic photos on smartphones. It allows a narrow field-of-view camera to capture wide-angle scenes by combining multiple overlapping shots.
concepts.recap_md: - Homographies are used to warp and align multiple images into a common reference frame.

We can use the estimated homographies to warp all of the images into a single camera view as shown in fig-panorama.
